lessons.examTip: Distinguish choropleth (shaded areas) from dot-density (individual dots) — FRQs ask you to justify which map type suits the data.
GIS questions ask what you can COMBINE — overlay population, elevation, and land use; know that GPS is collection, GIS is analysis.
Vernacular/perceptual regions (like 'the South') are defined by perception, not data — students confuse these with formal regions.
Cultural landscape = the visible imprint of culture on land; Sequent Occupance describes layers of successive cultures — know both terms with examples.
Gravity model: interaction ∝ (Pop₁ × Pop₂) / Distance² — larger cities pull more; increasing distance reduces interaction exponentially.
Physiological density = population / arable land — higher than arithmetic in Egypt (most land is desert); always specify which density.
Stage 5 (sub-replacement fertility) is NOT on all versions of the DTM — know that Japan and Germany are examples; NIR < 0 in Stage 5.
Wide base = Stage 2/3 (high youth, high future growth); narrow base = Stage 4/5 (aging population, strain on social services).
Malthus said population outruns food (pessimist); Boserup said necessity drives agricultural innovation (optimist) — FRQs ask you to apply both to a scenario.
Intervening opportunity (better option found en route) vs. intervening obstacle (barrier that stops migration) — students mix these up constantly.
Refugees cross international borders; IDPs (Internally Displaced Persons) stay within their country — this distinction matters for FRQ scoring.
Remittances can exceed foreign aid in developing nations — brain drain and remittances are two sides of the same migration coin.
Cultural hearths are origin points of innovation (Mesopotamia, Nile Valley, Indus Valley) — distinguish hearth from cultural diffusion pathway.
Contagious = spreads like a disease (contact); Hierarchical = jumps city-to-city; Stimulus = idea adopts but adapts (McDonald's goes local) — know all four.
Indo-European is the largest family; within it, Romance vs. Germanic vs. Slavic branches — Swahili is an example of a lingua franca, not a family.
Universalizing religions (Christianity, Islam, Buddhism) actively seek converts; Ethnic religions (Judaism, Hinduism) are tied to place/ethnicity — this is a key MCQ distinction.
Ethnic enclaves preserve culture (Little Italy, Chinatown) — distinguish from ghettos (forced segregation); FRQs ask you to identify which and explain why.
Gender inequality index and female education rates appear in development-themed FRQs — connect to DTM Stage and fertility rate.
The Kurds are the classic stateless nation example; the Arab nation spans multiple states — don't confuse 'state' (political unit) with 'nation' (cultural group).
Superimposed boundaries were drawn by outside powers ignoring cultural groups (Africa's colonial borders) — this is the root cause of many African conflicts.

topics: Compact, elongated, fragmented, prorupted, perforated states
lessons.examTip: Prorupted states have a panhandle giving access to resources or sea; Perforated states completely surround another (South Africa surrounds Lesotho).
Centripetal forces unite (common language, national anthem); centrifugal forces divide (ethnic conflict, regional autonomy demands) — always give a specific example.
Supranationalism = states giving up some sovereignty to a larger body; Brexit is the prime example of a state reasserting sovereignty over supranational membership.
Gerrymandering involves 'cracking' (split opponent voters) or 'packing' (concentrate opponent voters) — FRQs show district maps and ask you to identify the technique.
First Ag Revolution = domestication (~10,000 BCE); Second = mechanization (18th c. Britain); Third = Green Revolution (20th c.) — know all three and their geographic hearths.
Von Thünen: intensive farming closest to market (dairy, vegetables), extensive farming farther out (grain, ranching) — the model assumes flat plain and single market.
Shifting cultivation (slash and burn) is subsistence and extensive; market gardening is commercial and intensive — map these terms to Von Thünen rings.
Green Revolution increased yields but also increased reliance on fertilizers and water — FRQs ask you to weigh benefits (less hunger) vs. costs (soil degradation, debt).
The Aral Sea shrinkage is the canonical example of unsustainable irrigation — rivers diverted for cotton farming caused an environmental catastrophe.
Central place theory: threshold (minimum population to support a service) vs. range (maximum distance customers travel) — larger threshold = higher order place.
Concentric Zone = rings from CBD; Sector = pie slices along transportation; Multiple Nuclei = several nodes — FRQs give a city diagram and ask you to identify the model.

lessons.lessonTitle: Latin American, SE Asian, and Sub-Saharan City Models
lessons.examTip: Griffin-Ford: spine of commercial activity radiating from CBD with elite housing along it, shanty towns (disamenity zones) at periphery — inverse of US model.
Edge cities (Tyson's Corner, VA) have more jobs than bedrooms — distinguish from bedroom communities (commuter suburbs with no job centers).
Squatter settlements (favelas, bustees, bidonvilles) lack legal title and formal services — know regional terms; FRQs ask you to propose a realistic improvement strategy.
Gentrification raises property values, displacing lower-income residents — FRQs ask you to identify winners and losers; New Urbanism advocates walkable, mixed-use design.
Rostow (optimistic ladder): traditional → take-off → drive to maturity; Wallerstein (critical): core exploits periphery — FRQs ask you to critique both models.
HDI combines income, education, and life expectancy — higher than GDP rank means good social programs (Cuba); lower means wealth without social investment (Gulf states).
Weber: locate at minimum transport cost for inputs + outputs; bulk-gaining industries locate near market; bulk-reducing industries locate near raw materials.
Maquiladoras (Mexico–US border) are the canonical SEZ example — cheap labor, lax regulation, export-oriented; commodity chains trace production from raw material to consumer.
Brundtland: 'meeting present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet their own' — quote this definition exactly; FRQs love asking about it.
Exigence = the urgency or problem that prompted the text; students often confuse it with purpose — exigence is WHY it was written NOW, purpose is WHAT the writer wants to achieve.
FRQ 2 (Rhetorical Analysis) always asks HOW choices affect the audience — never just label a device; explain the effect on the specific audience in context.
A complex thesis acknowledges complexity or tension — 'while X, Y because Z' scores higher than a simple assertion; practice writing nuanced claims, not just pro/con.

topics: Claims of fact, value, and policy
lessons.examTip: Claims of policy argue 'should' — these require evidence for both the problem AND the solution; FRQ 3 (Argument) is almost always a policy claim.
Evidence alone earns no points — commentary explaining HOW the evidence supports your claim is what differentiates a 4 from a 6 on the argument FRQ.
Acknowledging a counterargument and then refuting or qualifying it shows sophistication — the 'complexity' point on the rubric requires engaging with tension, not ignoring it.

topics: Ad hominem, false dichotomy, slippery slope
lessons.examTip: MCQ passages often contain deliberate fallacies — identify the specific name and explain why it undermines the argument's logic, not just 'it's wrong'.
Ethos isn't just about credentials — a writer builds ethos by conceding points fairly, using precise language, and demonstrating knowledge; look for all three in FRQ passages.
Logos questions ask about the STRUCTURE of the argument — inductive (specific → general) vs. deductive (general → specific); deductive is stronger if the premises are accepted.
Pathos is NOT manipulation — it becomes manipulative only when it substitutes for evidence; in rhetorical analysis, explain which emotion is triggered and why it's effective here.
Kairos = the opportune moment — King's 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' has high kairos because it responds directly to a published letter of criticism; timeliness strengthens ethos.
Periodic sentence withholds the main clause until the end (creates suspense); cumulative adds details after main clause (builds picture) — both appear on MCQ with effect questions.
Tone shift questions: identify the before-tone, after-tone, and the turning word/phrase that signals the shift — 'yet', 'however', 'but' often mark the pivot.
FRQ rhetorical analysis rarely rewards just naming 'metaphor' — explain what is being compared and how the comparison advances the author's argument or characterization.
In synthesis and argument FRQs, your own voice matters — avoid passive constructions and hedging language like 'it could be argued'; be direct and assertive in your prose.
Synthesis FRQ requires using AT LEAST 3 of 6–7 provided sources — cite as (Source A) or (Source B); using 4+ sources distinguishes a 5 from a 6.
The most common synthesis mistake: summarizing each source in a separate paragraph instead of weaving them into your own argument — sources should support YOU, not the other way around.
You do NOT use MLA/APA format on the AP exam — simply write '(Source C)' or 'as the graph in Source D shows'; no bibliography required.
The argument FRQ prompt gives you a statement to defend, challenge, or qualify — 'qualify' (agree with conditions) is the most sophisticated position and scores highest.
Each body paragraph needs its own mini-claim (not just a topic sentence) that connects back to the thesis — a paragraph about evidence with no claim earns no reasoning points.
MCQ grammar questions: eliminate passive voice, vague pronouns, and dangling modifiers — these are the three most tested editing issues on the multiple-choice section.

topics: Exposition, rising action, climax, falling action
lessons.examTip: FRQ 1 (prose analysis) focuses on HOW narrative choices create meaning — don't retell the plot; identify the specific structural choice and explain its effect.
Foil questions: explain what the contrasting character REVEALS about the protagonist — never describe the foil in isolation; always link back to the main character's traits.
Unreliable narrator questions appear on MCQ — look for internal contradictions, self-serving logic, or dramatic irony where readers know more than the narrator.
Pathetic fallacy = nature reflects character's emotion (storm during grief) — FRQs ask how setting contributes to theme, not just describe what it looks like.
A symbol must be earned by context — don't just call the color green 'hope'; trace how the text builds that symbolic meaning through repetition and contrast.
Shakespearean sonnet: 3 quatrains + couplet; the volta (turn) often occurs at line 9 or in the couplet — FRQ poetry questions frequently ask about the effect of the volta.
Scansion errors are common: 'iambic pentameter' = 5 iambs (da-DUM) per line = 10 syllables — a spondee (DUM-DUM) or pyrrhic substitution signals stress emphasis.
Imagery analysis: identify the sense, describe the specific image, then explain what emotional/thematic meaning it creates — three steps, not just one label.
A conceit extends a metaphor throughout the poem (Donne's compass conceit) — FRQs ask you to trace HOW the comparison develops and WHERE it breaks down or complicates.
Never say 'the poet feels' — say 'the speaker' or 'the narrator'; the speaker is a persona, not necessarily the author; FRQ graders deduct for conflating the two.
Theme is a STATEMENT, not a word — not 'death' but 'confronting mortality forces recognition of what we value in life'; complexity comes from tension between competing themes.
FRQ 3 (literary argument) asks you to choose your own text — prepare 3–4 complex novels deeply; breadth of novels matters less than depth of analysis.
Hamartia is a 'fatal flaw' — but in complex texts it's often a strength taken too far (Macbeth's ambition); FRQs reward this nuanced interpretation.
Subplots often mirror or invert the main plot's theme — the Gloucester subplot in Lear mirrors Lear's blindness theme; FRQs give points for connecting subplot to main theme.
Contextualize but don't reduce — a good FRQ argument uses historical context to illuminate the text's meaning, not to replace close reading with plot summary.
Strongest literary thesis format: 'In [work], [author] uses [technique] to suggest [complex thematic claim]' — the claim must be ARGUABLE, not just observable.
Embed short quotes (4 words or fewer) mid-sentence with analysis — avoid block quotes; each quoted word should be earning its place by proving your specific claim.
The '1 complexity point' on the rubric requires going beyond a simple claim — complicate your thesis by acknowledging where the text challenges or complicates your reading.
